subject: ent
title: Epistaxis

steps.tx: Most nosebleeds arise anteriorly from **Kiesselbach plexus** in Little area where septal vessels anastomose superficially, provoked by picking, dry air, rhinitis and trauma, especially in children and young adults. Anterior bleeds ooze from one nostril and yield to pressure. Posterior bleeds (sphenopalatine territory) in older hypertensive or anticoagulated patients run down the throat, resist pressure and threaten airway and blood loss.
steps.say: Front bleeds drip out and squeeze shut. Back bleeds pour down throats of older patients and endanger airways.

steps.tx: First aid is universal and examined: sit up leaning **forward**, pinch the soft nose (not bony bridge) continuously for 10 to 15 minutes, spit blood, breathe through mouth, and avoid blowing afterwards. Ice adds little. Failure proceeds to examination with suction, vasoconstrictor and anaesthetic spray, then silver nitrate cautery only to a visible anterior point and never both septal sides at once (perforation risk).
steps.say: Lean forward, pinch soft nose fifteen minutes. Cauterise one septal side only or you perforate it.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Persistent bleeding needs packing: absorbable materials or inflatable anterior packs, and posterior packs or balloons for back bleeds with admission, oxygen monitoring and antibiotics per protocol because of toxic shock and hypoxia risks. Check haemoglobin, coagulation and anticoagulant burden (warfarin, DOACs, antiplatelets) and blood pressure after control, not as substitute for local control.
steps.say: Packed noses (especially posterior) get admitted and monitored. Check blood count, clotting drugs and pressure after stopping flow.

steps.tx: Refractory bleeds escalate to endoscopic **sphenopalatine artery** ligation or cautery in theatre, anterior ethmoid control for high bleeds, and interventional embolisation in selected patients unfit or failing surgery (stroke and blindness risks counselled). Ligation has largely replaced external carotid approaches. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and tumours (juvenile angiofibroma in adolescent males) underlie recurrent patterns needing specialist pathways.
steps.say: Unstoppable back bleeds get the sphenopalatine artery tied endoscopically. Teenage boys with recurrent bleeds may harbour angiofibroma.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Recurrent unilateral bleeds with obstruction demand nasendoscopy for tumours, septal spurs or telangiectasia; blood dyscrasia workup follows bilateral recurrent childhood patterns. Discharge advice (no blowing, sneezing open mouth, humidification, petroleum jelly) prevents early rebleeds. Anticoagulants are restarted by balancing thrombotic risk with cardiology or haematology input.
steps.say: One sided recurrent bleeds need scope for lumps. Restart blood thinners by balancing clot versus bleed with specialists.
